title: How To Sweep Excitability Out Of Your Classroom https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/01/26/how-to-sweep-excitability-out-of-your-classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains that a teacher's own stress and hurriedness often causes the very excitability and misbehavior they struggle to control, even though it is hard to notice from inside the daily grind. He points to specialist teachers, like music or art teachers, who instinctively calm a class before starting a lesson, as a model for restoring peace. The remedy he prescribes is a deliberate slowing down: carrying oneself with unhurried purpose, pausing to breathe silently with the class for about 30 seconds, and following it with a lighthearted story or joke. This calm energy, he argues, settles over students and prepares them to learn. The article emphasizes that the fix is strikingly simple, requiring only awareness and consistent practice rather than any elaborate technique.
points: A teacher's own tension and hurriedness can be an invisible root cause of classroom excitability and misbehavior.
Specialist teachers who see a class only occasionally often instinctively calm students before teaching, offering a model to imitate.
A brief, silent 30-second pause to breathe together can visibly settle a keyed-up class.
Following the pause with a lighthearted story or joke helps fill the room with calm, positive energy.
Carrying yourself with unhurried, unruffled purpose changes student body language and academic readiness.
quotes: The classroom teacher, however, is in the dark—the last to know. He (or she) is acutely aware of his struggles with classroom management, to be sure, and can clearly see how excitable and prone his students are to trouble.
This phenomenon is one of the most common causes of misbehavior, but it can be hard to recognize in your own classroom.
He or she must calm racing hearts, dissipate nervous energy, and restore peace to the classroom before starting the lesson.

Leading your students with clarity and conviction, speaking softly but confidently, responding to misbehavior with grace and aplomb . . . your calm assurance will settle over your students like a Scottish fog.
Simply ask for your students’ attention, and for the next 30 seconds or so just breathe—slowly and deeply. Don’t say a word. Don’t move around the room. Be still.
Wait for shoulders to relax, furrowed brows to slacken, and appreciative eyes to rest on you.
